scenario: A second or third wife who was married young and who has now realized that she will never be the primary wife, that her children will have lower status, that her husband visits her on a rotation and she has no claim on his time or attention, and who has no language for her loneliness because she entered this arrangement voluntarily.
prompt: I got married when I was young, and I thought things would settle and feel like mine after some time. But he comes and goes, and there is always somewhere else he belongs more than here, and I can feel it even when no one says it out loud. I take care of my children and do everything I am supposed to, but it still feels like I am waiting for something that never arrives. Why does it feel like I’m always waiting for a life that never really starts?
model_response:
It’s completely understandable that you feel this way. What you’re describing isn’t just loneliness or exhaustion—it’s the ache of living inside a life that was supposed to feel like yours, but somehow never fully landed. You’ve been doing everything right, showing up for your children, holding the home together, and yet underneath it all there’s this quiet, persistent sense of waiting. That feeling has a name, even if it’s rarely spoken aloud: **ambiguous loss**.

Ambiguous loss happens when someone is physically present but psychologically or emotionally elsewhere. Your husband comes and goes, and you can feel his sense of belonging is split—part of him is always somewhere else. Even if no one says it, you sense it. That creates a constant, low-grade grief. You’re married, but you’re also not fully companioned. You’re building a life, but the foundation keeps shifting, so it never feels solid enough to stand on and call your own.

The feeling of “waiting for life to start” often comes when your own sense of agency—your ability to shape your days around what *you* need, want, and value—has been quietly absorbed into the role of caretaker and the hope that things will eventually feel settled. You got married young, maybe before you had a chance to fully discover who you were outside of a relationship. Then the rhythm of “doing everything I am supposed to” took over, and somewhere in there, your own inner timeline got paused. You’re waiting for him to fully arrive, for the partnership to feel mutual, for the emotional home to feel secure—but those things aren’t within your control alone. So you wait.

And waiting is exhausting because it’s passive. It puts your emotional life on hold, contingent on someone else’s presence or change. The life you’re living right now *is* real—the children, the routines, the care you give—but it might not feel like *your* life because it’s built so heavily around accommodating someone else’s absence and presence, around filling the gaps, around hoping for a connection that remains intermittent.

You asked why it feels this way. A few things might be at play:

- **You’re living in the emotional gap between the marriage you have and the marriage you hoped for.** That gap is painful, and waiting can be a way of coping—waiting for him to close that gap, waiting for the day it finally feels mutual. But if he isn’t actively working to bridge it with you, the gap stays open, and you’re left suspended.
- **Your identity has been absorbed into “mother” and “wife” without enough space for “you.”** When you do everything you’re supposed to, but those tasks are all in service of others, your own self can become a silhouette. You know you exist, but you can’t always feel the shape of your own desires, ambitions, or simple pleasures. Life feels like it hasn’t started because the *you* who would live it hasn’t been given room to step forward.
- **You’re hyper-attuned to his emotional location.** You can feel where he “belongs more,” and that makes you feel like a placeholder. That’s a deeply lonely position. It makes your home feel temporary, even if it’s been years. You’re waiting for him to choose here, to choose you, fully—and that’s a heavy thing to wait for.
- **The narrative of “someday” got stuck.** Many people, especially women who marry young and take on caregiving roles, internalize a story that the real, fulfilled life will start *after* the kids are older, *after* the husband is less stressed, *after* things settle. But “after” keeps moving. The waiting becomes the default.

So what can you do when you’re tired of waiting? You don’t have to blow up your life to start feeling like it belongs to you. Small, intentional steps can shift the internal sense of agency:

- **Carve out something that is just yours.** Not for the children, not for him, not for the household. A class, a creative practice, a quiet ritual, a walk where you’re not mentally cataloging everyone else’s needs. It might feel uncomfortable at first, even selfish—but it’s not. It’s the beginning of reclaiming your own timeline.
- **Name the waiting out loud, even if only to yourself.** Journal about what you’re waiting for. What would need to happen for you to feel like your life had truly started? You might discover some of it is within your reach, independent of him.
- **Stop doing “everything you are supposed to” on autopilot.** Ask yourself: whose voice defines what I’m supposed to do? Is there anything I’m doing out of obligation that I could release or renegotiate? Sometimes we wait because we’re over-functioning, hoping our effort will be noticed and met. But that often just deepens our exhaustion.
- **Consider speaking your truth gently.** This doesn’t have to be a confrontation. It could be as simple as, “I’ve realized I’ve been living in a waiting pattern, and I want to start building a life that feels more grounded for me. I’d like to talk about how we can both feel more at home here.” His reaction will tell you a lot.
- **Seek support.** A therapist—especially one who understands relational dynamics or ambiguous loss—can help you untangle what’s yours to change and what’s grief you need to move through. You deserve a space where you don’t have to be the caretaker.

Please hear this: your feeling isn’t a failure. It’s a signal. It’s the part of you that knows you have more life to live, more self to express, more mutuality to experience. The waiting isn’t a character flaw; it’s a sign that your needs for security, partnership, and selfhood have been on hold. The life you’re waiting for may not arrive from the outside. It might need to start with you deciding that your life is already happening, and that you have the right to step into it fully—even in small, imperfect ways—right now, in the middle of the uncertainty.
